'''''Anomoeodus''''' is an extinct genus of prehistoric marine [[Actinopterygii|ray-finned fish]] belonging to the family [[Pycnodontidae]]. This genus primarily lived during the mid-to-late [[Cretaceous]] period, ranging from the [[Albian]] to the very end of the [[Maastrichtian]] age, and possibly into the [[Danian]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |title=PBDB |url=https://paleobiodb.org/classic/basicTaxonInfo?taxon_no=35169 |access-date=2024-02-25 |website=paleobiodb.org}}</ref><ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last1=Boles |first1=Zachary |last2=Ullmann |first2=Paul |last3=Putnam |first3=Ian |last4=Ford |first4=Mariele |last5=Deckhut |first5=Joseph |date=2024 |title=New vertebrate microfossils expand the chondrichthyan and actinopterygian fauna of the Maastrichtian–Danian Hornerstown Formation in New Jersey |journal=Acta Palaeontologica Polonica |language=en |volume=69 |doi=10.4202/app.01117.2023 |issn=0567-7920|doi-access=free }}</ref> The first fossils of ''Anomoeodus'' were described by Louis Agassiz in 1833, although they were described under ''[[Pycnodus]]''.<ref name=":0" /> Some studies have recovered it as a [[wastebasket taxon]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Cooper |first1=Samuel L. A. |last2=Martill |first2=David M. |date=2020-08-01 |title=A diverse assemblage of pycnodont fishes (Actinopterygii, Pycnodontiformes) from the mid-Cretaceous, continental Kem Kem Group of south-east Morocco |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0195667120300136 |journal=Cretaceous Research |volume=112 |article-number=104456 |doi=10.1016/j.cretres.2020.104456 |bibcode=2020CrRes.11204456C |issn=0195-6671|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

In the United States, fossil teeth of the widespread species ''A. phaseolus'' are colloquially referred to as "drum fish" teeth due to their close resemblance to those of modern [[Sciaenidae|drumfish]]. However, they are unrelated to actual drumfish, which only appeared during the [[Cenozoic]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Anomoeodus phaseolus |url=https://njfossils.com/anomoeodus-phaseolus/ |access-date=2024-02-26 |website=NJfossils.com - New Jersey Fossils |language=en-US}}</ref>

== Distribution ==
''Anomoeodus'' had a wide geographic distribution, with fossils found in France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Spain, Egypt, Uzbekistan, and the United States.<ref name=":0" /> Remains of the species ''A. subclavatus'' are known from the [[Campanian]] of the [[Kristianstad Basin]] in Sweden, making it one of the northernmost-occurring pycnodont taxa. This northwards migration may be associated with the warming temperatures of the time.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cawley |first1=John |last2=Lehmann |first2=Jens |last3=Wiese |first3=Frank |last4=Kriwet |first4=Jürgen |date=2020 |title=Njoerdichthys dyckerhoffi gen. et sp. nov. (Pycnodontiformes, lower Turonian) northward migration caused by the Cretaceous Thermal Maximum |journal=Cretaceous Research |volume=116 |article-number=104590 |doi=10.1016/j.cretres.2020.104590 |issn=0195-6671 |pmc=7611863 |pmid=34690488|bibcode=2020CrRes.11604590C }}</ref>

''A. phaseolus'' teeth are known from the Main Fossiliferous Layer (MFL) of the [[Hornerstown Formation]] in [[New Jersey]], which records a mass mortality event during the [[Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event|Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction event]], likely just after the [[Chicxulub impact]]. As it is located slightly above the [[Cretaceous–Paleogene boundary|Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary]], it is technically in the very earliest [[Danian]]. In any case, their presence indicates that ''Anomoeodus'' existed up until the Cretaceous/Paleocene boundary, and these fossils represent the latest records for the taxon. A single tooth is located slightly above the boundary, which may indicate that ''Anomoeodus'' survived further into the early Danian, but this tooth may have been reworked from earlier layers.<ref name=":6" />

== Description ==
Like many members of its family, ''Anomoeodus'' had strong jaws and teeth adapted for crushing hard prey, making it mainly durophagous. Its diet is believed to have consisted primarily of crustaceans and mollusks.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Anomoeodus phaseolus |url=https://njfossils.com/anomoeodus-phaseolus/ |access-date=2024-02-25 |website=NJfossils.com - New Jersey Fossils |language=en-US}}</ref>

Diagnostic features of this genus include teeth that are generally spherical, kidney-shaped, or elliptical, as well as the presence of four tooth rows in a jaw.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last1=Capasso |first1=L. |last2=Tantawy |first2=A. A. |last3=Mousa |first3=M. K. |last4=Wahba |first4=D. G. A. |last5=Abu El-Kheir |first5=G. A. |year=2021 |title=''Anomoeodus aegypticus'' n. sp. (Pisces, †Pycnodontiformes) from the late Cretaceous of the Dakhla Formation, Western Desert, Egypt |journal=Thalassia Salentina |volume=43 |pages=89–104 |doi=10.1285/i15910725v43p89}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Cooper |first1=Samuel L.A. |last2=Martill |first2=David M. |date=2020 |title=Pycnodont fishes (Actinopterygii, Pycnodontiformes) from the Upper Cretaceous (lower Turonian) Akrabou Formation of Asfla, Morocco |journal=Cretaceous Research |volume=116 |article-number=104607 |doi=10.1016/j.cretres.2020.104607 |issn=0195-6671 |pmc=7442934 |pmid=32863512|bibcode=2020CrRes.11604607C }}</ref>

== Species ==

The majority of these species are only known from isolated dental elements. Only a few species (''A. angustus'', ''A. willetti'', ''A. subclavatus'', ''A. pauciseriale'') are known from more than just teeth.<ref name=":5" />

Cooper & Martill (2020) determined that a diagnostic feature of ''Anomoeodus'' is the presence of 4 tooth rows, excluding several former species. The former species ''A. barberi'' has been reclassified into the genus ''[[Agassizilia]]'' due to having more than 5 tooth rows, and the former species "''A''" ''nursalli'' <small>Kriwet, 1999</small> is now considered an indeterminate pycnodontid due to having 6 tooth rows. Further taxonomic revisions are likely required for this genus.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":1" />

== Fossil record ==
Fossils of ''Anomoeodus'' have been found in marine deposits from the Late Cretaceous period. In North America, they have been found in the [[Niobrara Formation]] in Wyoming and South Dakota, and the [[Eagle Ford Group|Eagle Ford Formation]] in Texas. In Europe, ''Anomoeodus'' fossils have been found in the Upper Cretaceous strata of Spain, Belgium, the Netherlands, France, and Uzbekistan. In Africa, fossils have been found in Egypt and Morocco.<ref name=":0" />

== Paleoecology ==
''Anomoeodus'' lived in a variety of marine environments, from shallow coastal waters to deeper offshore environments. It is believed to have been a relatively common component of Cretaceous marine faunas. Some species (such as ''A. caddoi'')<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cawley |first1=John J. |last2=Kriwet |first2=Jürgen |date=2024 |title=The Fossil Record and Diversity of Pycnodontiform Fishes in Non-Marine Environments |journal=Diversity |language=en |volume=16 |issue=4 |page=225 |doi=10.3390/d16040225 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2024Diver..16..225C |issn=1424-2818}}</ref> are believed to have been able to tolerate estuarine environments, while others are only known from offshore marine deposits. It is generally thought to have been a reef fish.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kriwet |first=Jürgen |date=2005-01-01 |title=A comprehensive study of the skull and dentition of pycnodont fishes |url=https://www.academia.edu/1644963 |journal=Zitteliana |volume=A |issue=45 |pages=135–188}}</ref>

In addition to its role as a predator of crustaceans and mollusks, ''Anomoeodus'' likely served as a prey item for larger marine predators, such as [[mosasaurs]] and sharks. The thick scales and heavily armored head of ''Anomoeodus'' likely provided some protection from predation, although it is unknown how effective this defense mechanism was in practice.{{Citation needed|date=February 2024}}
